summary: Weekly POC check-in to review throughput results and tuning changes. Discussed continuous batching tweaks, concurrency targets, queueing strategy, and next steps for a 4-hour stress benchmark. Agreed to try slightly higher concurrency with adaptive queue window and to measure KV cache hit rate impact.
transcript:
00:00 Alex Morgan: hey everyone good afternoon, um we'll do a quick sync on the throughput experiments we ran last week
00:07 Priya Rao: hi, thanks, excited to hear, we had the team run the nightly load last night so should have the logs
00:12 Sam Patel: cool, quick agenda, recap of numbers, what we tuned (batch windows, concurrency), queueing ideas, next steps
00:19 Marcus Lee: quick note from our side, we hit a weird tail latency spike around 11:30pm, looked like queuing backlog, not sure if it's batch related
00:30 Alex Morgan: ok let's start with the numbers, Sam do you have the throughput table?
00:35 Sam Patel: yeah so baseline (stock config) avg tokens/sec per GPU was ~9.2k, with 64-token prompt avg, p50 latency 120ms p95 420ms, p99 1.1s, after enabling continuous batching + 30ms window we saw tokens/sec jump to 12.8k, p50 similar, p95 down to 380ms but p99 still around 950ms
01:05 Elena Torres: mmh those p99s are the problematic ones for our SLAs, we need <800ms for critical routes
01:12 Priya Rao: question, was KV cache warm during that run? we rely heavily on prefix caching for dialogs
01:17 Sam Patel: good call, KV cache hit rate was about 58% during the experiment, we think lower than expected because of short-lived test sessions and varying user ids
01:28 Alex Morgan: ok so two levers: increase concurrency and also improve cache locality or sticky routing so the cache warms better
01:36 Marcus Lee: when you say increase concurrency you mean more simultaneous requests per model instance or more worker processes?
01:42 Sam Patel: more simultaneous in-flight tokens per GPU (increase model concurrency), also align batch timeout, if timeout too low we under-batch, too high we increase latency tail
01:52 Tom Wu: we were worried increasing concurrency would blow up out costs, was that measured?
01:57 Sam Patel: yes there's a cost tradeoff, but our recommendation is incremental: raise concurrency in small steps and monitor p50/p95/p99, also use priority queue for critical routes to avoid head-of-line blocking
02:10 Priya Rao: can you expand on the priority queue idea?
02:14 Jules Kim: sure, basically maintain separate queues per priority class and give small reserved concurrency to high-priority flows. If low-priority backlog grows it won't push high-priority into the tail. This is a lightweight change in the router layer
02:28 Alex Morgan: practical suggestion: reserve 25% of concurrency for high-priority endpoints, let the rest be elastic for normal traffic, that often clears p99s
02:37 Marcus Lee: ok interesting. For autoscaling, we saw scale-up latency of about 2m30s which caused bursts to queue. Any way to smooth that?
02:47 Sam Patel: yes, warm pools and burst capacity help, and smaller scale steps with aggressive pre-warming based on predictive signals. Redwood Dedicated offers reserved pools and burst capacity to cover those spikes
03:00 Elena Torres: can we simulate that quickly? what config do you suggest?
03:04 Sam Patel: start with concurrency +15% over baseline per GPU, batch window 40ms, reserve concurrency 20-25% for critical routes, enable keep-warm instances at min 2 nodes during business hours
03:16 Priya Rao: will that change our KV cache behavior?
03:19 Sam Patel: warm instances help cache locality, and also sticky routing by user id will increase hit rate; sticky routing means small hash-based affinity for 30m sessions
03:29 Marcus Lee: earlier you mentioned queue window, is that the same as batch window?
03:32 Sam Patel: similar, queue window = how long router holds requests to build a batch; batch window sometimes adaptive based on current QPS
03:38 Tom Wu: we saw some transcripts where the recognizer spelled Redwood as redwoo, there are little transcribe typos in the logs, nothing critical
03:43 Alex Morgan: haha yeah auto transcribe... back to throughput, did you capture memory/GPU util?
03:47 Marcus Lee: we collected util, GPUs avg util 67% baseline, jumped to 82% with continuous batching config, which is good but thermal/power ceilings may bite
03:58 Priya Rao: what's our target throughput to consider this POC successful? we said earlier 2x baseline right?
04:04 Alex Morgan: I think target was 1.8-2x baseline while keeping p95 < 450ms and p99 < 800ms for critical endpoints
04:14 Sam Patel: current runs are at ~1.4x baseline; cache fixes + reserved concurrency should get us closer to 1.7-1.9x in next run
04:22 Elena Torres: about the tail spikes at 11:30pm, we saw a correlated cron job that kicks heavy batch of small requests, that might cause starvation
04:33 Alex Morgan: do we have an option to throttle background jobs or mark them as low priority?
04:36 Marcus Lee: yes we can change internal flags, we can gate cron to low-priority queue, would be a quick config change
04:42 Tom Wu: any security implications for sticky routing or affinity? we need to make sure encryption/KMS, session tokens are handled right
04:48 Sam Patel: nothing new there, affinity is routing layer only, data-in-flight still encrypted, but we will document how tokens are hashed and ensure we don't persist PII in the affinity keys
04:59 Priya Rao: good that's important for compliance (we're SOC2-aligned internally), also need audit logs for any routing changes
05:06 Alex Morgan: Redwood can provide audit trails for rollouts and router config changes, we'll attach the security doc to next email
05:13 Marcus Lee: on observability, can you add 1-minute histograms for queue length and batch sizes? that will help root cause
05:20 Sam Patel: yes we'll add hist metrics and a Grafana dashboard sample, include batch size distribution and KV hit-rate over time
05:29 Alex Morgan: great, high-level plan: 1) try the conservative concurrency bump + sticky routing + reserved concurrency 2) run 4-hour stress test capturing p50/p95/p99, batch sizes, KV hit-rate, GPU util 3) review results next sync
05:48 Priya Rao: for the 4-hour run, we also want to test failure scenarios: a node drop and a sudden 3x burst, to see how graceful fallback works
05:58 Sam Patel: agreed we'll script the chaos scenarios into the benchmark (node termination + high short burst), Redwood router has fallback policies to degrade to a smaller model if capacity constrained
06:12 Tom Wu: you mentioned fallback to smaller models, does that change the output quality we should expect? product worry here
06:17 Sam Patel: yes there's a quality/cost tradeoff; fallback is last resort and we would prefer to prioritize critical routes first before degrading; we'll show sample regression evals if we need to demonstrate quality delta
06:30 Priya Rao: what's the timeline for the next run? can we do it by end of week?
06:34 Alex Morgan: we said Jan 25 for config, Jan 28 for results, so a run in the 26-27 window would be ideal
06:42 Marcus Lee: one operational question: any changes needed to our ingress or LB to support sticky routing?
06:46 Sam Patel: only minor header changes for affinity cookie or hash key; we'll give an implementation note, nothing heavy at infra layer
06:53 Elena Torres: I'll follow up to schedule the deep-dive with our SREs and include the power/thermal team because of GPU util implications
06:59 Alex Morgan: perfect, we'll send the tuned config and the benchmark harness, Sam will lead the benchmark script and I'll attach security docs and our recommended priority settings
07:09 Priya Rao: thanks everyone, this was productive
07:11 Alex Morgan: thanks all, we'll chat soon - adjourn
07:14 [call ends]
